sections.h2: Choosing a sale route in Garland
sections.html:
A cash sale is quickest, a listing takes longest, and selling on your own sits between. Let the condition of the house and whether tenants live in it drive the choice.

Garland runs a permit program for single-family and short-term rentals through its Code Compliance Department. If your house is a rental, that program will shape a sale more than any market swing. An investor can buy as-is and sort out the permit change afterward, while a retail buyer usually expects an inspected, move-in ready home.

  • Cash sale: no showings or repair haggling, with a closing day you pick.
  • Listing: more buyers see it, and you carry prep work and inspection requests.
  • Owner sale: you manage the contract, disclosures and title work yourself.

sections.h2: Rental permit rules that affect a sale
sections.html:
Every single-family rental in Garland, duplexes included, needs a permit from Code Compliance. The permit cannot be assigned or transferred, so a buyer who keeps renting the house must apply in their own name.

Garland rental permit terms
Permit typeAnnual feeInspection and other terms
Single-family rental$65, with renewals at $250 from Oct. 1, 2026Full inspection at each change of tenancy, unless the property is certified
Short-term rental$500Floor plan and proof of insurance; annual inspection for renewal

The city council has also looked at treating short-term rentals as their own land use, generally allowed by right only in Light Commercial and Heavy Commercial districts and in planned development districts that expressly allow it. Call Code Compliance at 972-485-6400 to ask whether that rule now applies to your address.

sections.h2: Can code violations stop a Garland sale?
sections.html:
No. Violations do not block a sale, but they can cool buyer interest and you should disclose them to anyone who asks. A cash buyer is often the easier match because the house is bought as-is.

If you have a notice of violation and need more time, contact your Code Compliance Officer. The department also takes requests through its online portal and the eAssist app, and the phone line is 972-485-6400. A short extension in writing is handy to give a buyer along with the notice.

  • Keep a copy of every notice and any extension.
  • Ask the officer what a reinspection would require.
  • Tell the title company about open violations before the contract is signed.

Delinquent tax follows the house. The year's lien takes hold on January 1, and clear title waits until the balance is paid.

Bills mail in October and go delinquent after January 31. Charges then build monthly, with the penalty reaching 12 percent by July 1. A collection attorney's fee can add up to 20 percent on top.

Relief may exist. Some collectors allow payment plans of up to 36 months on a homestead, and a written request can seek penalty relief if you meet the printed deadlines. Ask the office that bills your Garland parcel for a payoff figure and its plan terms. At closing, the title company pays the balance out of your proceeds, so you do not need cash up front.

sections.h2: What happens at a Texas tax sale
sections.html:
A constable or an agent of the taxing unit auctions the property. No statewide list exists, so watch the county clerk and tax office websites for notices.

Former owners of homestead, farm or mineral property may buy it back for two years after the purchaser's deed is filed. The premium is 25 percent in year one or 50 percent in year two, on top of the bid and costs. Other property carries a 180-day window. Surplus sale money can be claimed for two years.

A sale you close first spares you that process. Request a current payoff, and ask whether suit has been filed.

First establish who owns it on paper. An heir missing from the recorded deed who wants the homestead exemption must give the appraisal district an ownership affidavit, the death certificate and a utility bill.

If the owner recorded a transfer on death deed, the property skips probate. A Lady Bird deed instead let the owner sell freely while alive. Without either, the county clerk can explain probate filings and small estate affidavits.

Heirs often prefer not to repair and list a house they do not live in, which makes a documented as-is cash sale a common choice.

sections.h2: Inspection timing and your closing date
sections.html:
For a single-family rental, a full inspection happens at each change of tenancy unless the property is certified. The owner must tell Code Compliance about the vacancy and book the appointment. A short-term rental needs an inspection every year to renew the permit.

Timing matters when a tenant is moving out of a house you are selling. A buyer planning to re-rent will want to know whether an inspection is pending, what it might flag, and who pays to fix it. A copy of each inspection report goes to the landlord or manager, so ask for the latest one and hand it to the buyer or the title company.

  • Ask Code Compliance, at 972-485-6400, about your permit status.
  • Request the most recent inspection report.
  • List any open items in the sale contract.

sections.h2: What a rental buyer should agree to
sections.html:
Settle who applies for the new permit, who pays for any inspection, and how existing tenants are treated. Those answers decide whether closing runs smoothly.

  • Whether the offer is as-is, including anything the city inspection might flag.
  • Whether the buyer takes over the lease and security deposit, or needs the house vacant.
  • Who covers the permit fee and the inspection at the change of tenancy.
  • The closing date and which title company will handle the funds.

Put every answer in the written contract. For a short-term rental, also confirm the buyer understands the annual inspection and insurance steps the city requires for renewal.

sections.h2: Someone is living in the house without a lease
sections.html:
Sometimes an owner can ask the sheriff or constable to remove an occupant without a lawsuit, if specific conditions hold. Property Code chapter 24B sets them, and the State Law Library eviction guide summarizes it.

  • The person refused to leave after a request.
  • The house was closed to the public when the person walked in.
  • You and the occupant are not in a pending suit over the property.
  • The occupant has never rented from you and is not kin.

Removing the wrong person can expose you to a lawsuit, so check every item. A former tenant goes through the regular justice court eviction instead. In both cases, tell prospective buyers about the occupant in writing. An investor may accept an occupied house where a retail buyer will not.

The seller signs before a notary, and the deed is then filed with the clerk serving the parcel's county. Recording charges vary, so get the total from the clerk or the title company.

A pending foreclosure notice makes its sale date a hard deadline, since notice is due at least 21 days in advance. Aim to close well before it.

Before the closing appointment, gather your photo ID, any lease and deposit records for a tenant-occupied house, and every city notice you have received. A cash sale skips lender appraisals and buyer financing, which removes two common causes of delay.

faqs.q: Can a Garland rental permit transfer to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. Permits cannot be assigned or transferred, so a buyer who rents the house needs a new one.

faqs.q: Are there new Garland short-term rental rules?
faqs.a: The city council has considered limiting short-term rentals to certain commercial and planned development districts. Call Garland Code Compliance at 972-485-6400 to learn whether it applies to your address.

faqs.q: What is the annual Garland rental permit fee?
faqs.a: A single-family rental permit is $65 a year, with renewals at $250 from October 1, 2026. Short-term rental permits are $500 a year.

faqs.q: When do Garland property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: A bill still open after January 31 is late, and charges begin the next day.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Garland house before a tax foreclosure auction?
faqs.a: Yes. Paying the taxes from closing proceeds clears the lien, and finishing ahead of an auction sidesteps redemption rules and added court costs.
